items.stem: What is the difference between an SLO and an SLA?

options.text: An SLO is an internal reliability target; an SLA is an external commitment often with consequences
options.rationale: Correct: SLOs are internal goals, SLAs are contractual promises to customers.

options.text: An SLO is contractual and an SLA is internal
They are two names for the same metric
options.rationale: They are distinct: target versus agreement.

options.text: An SLA is a single measurement and an SLO is a dashboard
options.rationale: Neither is defined by being a measurement or a dashboard.

items.explanation: Correct: SLOs are internal goals, SLAs are contractual promises to customers.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about error budgets are correct?

options.text: An error budget is the allowed unreliability implied by the SLO
options.rationale: Correct: a 99.9% SLO implies a 0.1% error budget.

options.text: When the budget is nearly spent, teams may slow risky releases to protect reliability
options.rationale: Correct: the budget is a shared signal for balancing change against stability.

options.text: A 100% SLO is ideal because it gives the largest error budget
options.rationale: A 100% SLO leaves no error budget and no room to ship changes.

options.text: Error budgets require alerting on every individual error
options.rationale: Good practice alerts on burn rate, not on each error.

options.text: An error budget is the number of engineers on call
options.rationale: It is a reliability allowance, not a staffing count.

items.explanation: Correct: a 99.9% SLO implies a 0.1% error budget.

items.stem: Why alert on error-budget burn rate rather than on every error?

options.text: Burn-rate alerting pages when loss is significant, reducing noise and alert fatigue
options.rationale: Correct: it focuses attention on meaningful budget consumption, not isolated errors.

options.text: Burn-rate alerts remove the need for any SLO
options.rationale: Burn rate is derived from the SLO and error budget.
No alerting strategy guarantees zero incidents.
It is part of monitoring, not a replacement.

items.explanation: Correct: it focuses attention on meaningful budget consumption, not isolated errors.
